hypothesis_tests.Question: Do average bills differ between bills with an insurance claim and bills without? (100% of patients are insured, so 'uninsured' cannot be tested)
hypothesis_tests.Test: Welch two-sample t-test (Mann-Whitney U agrees: p = 0.155)
hypothesis_tests.Conclusion: Mean bill 154,838 RWF with claim vs 155,903 RWF without (-1,065).
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.154); effect size -0.013 is negligible. Mean bill 154,838 RWF with claim vs 155,903 RWF without (-1,065).

hypothesis_tests.Question: Do bills paid via the 'Insurance' method differ from other payment methods?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.661); effect size 0.004 is negligible. 155,417 vs 155,070 RWF.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does patient satisfaction differ across the 20 facilities?
hypothesis_tests.H0: Median rating identical in all facilities
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.795); effect size 0.008 is negligible. Facility means 2.76–3.19.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does satisfaction differ across the 10 department types?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.878); effect size 0.003 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Do admission rates differ between age groups?
hypothesis_tests.H0: Admission rate equal across the 7 age groups
hypothesis_tests.H1: At least one age group differs
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.065); effect size 0.049 is negligible. Rates 9.4%–13.9%.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does satisfaction depend on disease severity?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.835); effect size 0.000 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does length of stay differ by diagnosis?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.538); effect size 0.005 is negligible. Mean LOS 5.3–5.9 d.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Is satisfaction related to billing outcome (recorded bill status)?
hypothesis_tests.H0: Rating equal across Paid / Partially Paid / Pending
hypothesis_tests.Test: Kruskal-Wallis H (Spearman ρ rating vs paid ratio = -0.001, p = 0.893)
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.716); effect size 0.000 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Are emergency visits admitted more often than other visits?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.406); effect size 0.012 is negligible. Emergency 11.2% vs other 12.0%.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Are severe cases admitted more often than mild cases?
hypothesis_tests.H0: Admission rate equal across severity levels
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.533); effect size 0.016 is negligible. Rates: Mild 11.7%, Moderate 11.1%, Severe 12.4%

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does chronic-disease prevalence differ by gender?
hypothesis_tests.H0: Prevalence equal for men and women
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.653); effect size 0.003 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does chronic-disease prevalence differ by age group?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.456); effect size 0.017 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Is the written comment related to the numeric rating?
hypothesis_tests.Conclusion: A valid feedback instrument should show strong association.
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.904); effect size 0.010 is negligible. A valid feedback instrument should show strong association.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does the claim approval rate differ between insurance providers?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.077); effect size 0.013 is negligible.

hypothesis_tests.Question: Does the share of the bill actually paid differ by payment method?
hypothesis_tests.Interpretation: No significant difference (p = 0.412); effect size 0.000 is negligible.

recommendations.Recommendation: Fix the data foundation before further modelling
recommendations.Evidence: Only 5,000 of 60,000 billed appointments exist in the Appointments table; 95% of appointments point to a department owned by another facility; no facility master, bed status or equipment availability fields.
recommendations.Strength of evidence: High — verified by direct key checks
recommendations.Suggested action: Re-extract Appointments for the full year; enforce Facility→Department→Doctor foreign keys; add Facility master, bed status and equipment condition fields.

recommendations.Recommendation: Stop using bill 'Status' as a collections indicator
recommendations.Evidence: 80% of bills are paid in full whatever Status says; 'Pending' bills have the same average payment ratio (90%) as 'Paid'.
recommendations.Suggested action: Derive Status from Amount vs AmountPaid in the billing system; reconcile Revenue_Summary (1.13 bn) with billing (9.31 bn).

recommendations.Recommendation: Target outreach with a rule-based list, not a predictive model
recommendations.Evidence: 6,662 patients (33.3%) meet the high-risk rule (65+/50–64 with chronic disease, obesity or underweight); only 1,498 had an appointment in 2026. Chronic disease affects 74.6% of patients but no demographic factor predicts it (AUC 0.51).
recommendations.Strength of evidence: Medium — rule is clinical logic; data cannot validate it
recommendations.Suggested action: Call-back / screening programme for the high-risk list, prioritising patients aged 65+ with a chronic condition and no 2026 visit; evaluate uptake to validate the rule.

recommendations.Recommendation: Redesign the feedback instrument and capture real drivers
recommendations.Evidence: Mean rating 2.99/5; 40% rate 1–2. Ratings are unrelated to comment text, diagnosis, billing, department, facility or any modelled variable (best R² ≈ 0).
recommendations.Strength of evidence: High (that data cannot explain satisfaction); drivers unknown
recommendations.Suggested action: Add wait time, staff courtesy, cleanliness, drug availability and discharge-time questions; validate comment/rating consistency; collect ≥ 348 ratings per facility to detect a 0.3-point difference with 80% power (currently ≈ 89).

recommendations.Recommendation: Do not rank facilities or departments on current ratings
recommendations.Evidence: Facility means 2.76–3.19, department means 2.76–3.02; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.80 (facilities), 0.88 (departments).
recommendations.Suggested action: Publish confidence intervals with any league table; investigate the lowest-rated sites only after the new instrument yields adequate samples.

recommendations.Evidence: Facility volumes range 217–278 (28% spread) while headcount is 61–64 everywhere; staff numbers do not track volume (ρ = -0.10). Doctor load is random (variance/mean 0.95), i.e. nobody is systematically overloaded.
recommendations.Strength of evidence: Medium — the volume gap is not statistically significant (p = 0.052) but is practically large
recommendations.Suggested action: Move toward a staffing ratio per 1,000 appointments; rebalance rotas from the quietest sites toward HF013/HF011 as a pilot; review monthly with a rolling 3-month workload index.

recommendations.Recommendation: Verify bed capacity before any bed-related investment
recommendations.Evidence: All 2,000 beds are flagged 'Available'; recorded admissions imply only ≈3.8% annual bed-day use.
recommendations.Strength of evidence: Low — Admissions table appears to be an extract
recommendations.Suggested action: Capture daily bed census; if the 4% figure holds, consolidate wards rather than expand.

recommendations.Evidence: Lab test type is unrelated to diagnosis (χ² p = 0.366) — e.g. malaria patients are not more likely to get a malaria test — while prescribing matches diagnosis 100%.
recommendations.Strength of evidence: Medium — may be a data-linkage artefact
recommendations.Suggested action: Audit test-ordering against diagnostic protocols; link lab orders to diagnosis codes.

recommendations.Recommendation: Collect the outstanding balance and clear pending claims
recommendations.Evidence: 0.92 bn RWF (9.9%) of billed amounts is unpaid; 21,028 claims worth 2.44 bn RWF are 'Pending' and only 50% of claims are approved (no difference by provider, p = 0.08).
recommendations.Suggested action: Weekly ageing report on outstanding balances; dedicated follow-up team for pending claims; agree turnaround SLAs with all four insurers; 0.64 bn RWF of 'Insurance'-method payments have no claim on file — reconcile.

recommendations.Recommendation: Budget on a flat baseline and manage volatility
recommendations.Evidence: 2027 forecast ≈ 1.10 bn RWF (92 M/month, 95% band ±68%); no trend is detectable (12 months cannot reveal seasonality), and revenue is only weakly tied to visit counts (r = 0.28).
recommendations.Suggested action: Set the budget at the forecast mean with a contingency reserve; analyse the Sep-2026 peak (146 M) and Dec-2026 trough (67 M) for one-off billing events; collect 24+ months before using seasonal models.

recommendations.Recommendation: Do not expand on current evidence — build the evidence
recommendations.Evidence: Demand is flat (no trend, ρ = -0.14), evenly spread across provinces (19.6%–20.5%) and departments; admissions cannot be predicted; facility locations and service-level data are missing.
recommendations.Suggested action: Add facility geography (district, ownership, type) and ServiceID on bills; re-run province-level demand vs capacity once available. Prioritise Cardiology and Radiology for a staffing review (highest forecast load index, ≈105–109), but treat as provisional.

f01_patient_profile.title: Who are HealthConnect's patients?
f01_patient_profile.interp: The register is balanced by gender (50.4% male) and spans all ages (mean 45.0 y). 74.6% of patients carry a chronic condition, split almost equally across asthma, hypertension and diabetes. Blood groups are near-uniform (χ² test for equal shares p = 0.382), which is unusual for a real population where O and A dominate — another sign the data are simulated.

f02_age_pyramid.title: Age pyramid of registered patients
f02_age_pyramid.interp: The pyramid is rectangular rather than the narrow-topped shape of a real East-African population: children under 15 are 16.4% and adults 65+ are 28.5% of patients. Male share stays between 49% and 53% in every five-year band, so neither sex is concentrated in any age group; this evenness is another indicator of synthetic data.

f03_chronic_by_age.title: Chronic-disease prevalence by age group
f03_chronic_by_age.interp: Chronic-disease prevalence is flat across age groups (range 73–76%; χ² p = 0.456) and between sexes (p = 0.653). The risk score therefore rises with age almost entirely through the age points themselves: 90% of patients 65+ are high-risk versus 0% of under-5s. In real populations chronic disease rises steeply with age, so the absence of a gradient is a data-quality limitation, not a clinical finding.

f04_insurance.title: Patients by insurance code (INS001–INS015)
f04_insurance.interp: Every patient holds one of 15 insurance codes in near-equal numbers (χ² for equal shares p = 0.777), so the insurance coverage rate is effectively 100% and no uninsured group exists to compare. Insurance matters instead at billing: 70.1% of bills carry a claim, and the claim usually covers only part of the bill (median coverage 75%).

f05_geography.title: Patients by province
f05_geography.interp: Western has the most registered patients (4,091, 20.5%) and Northern the fewest (3,923); the spread is modest (χ² for equal shares p = 0.238). Every province contains exactly six districts, so near-equal shares are structural rather than a demand signal. The map is schematic: the data contain no coordinates or boundary files, so bubbles sit at approximate province centroids.

f06_patient_growth.title: Cumulative unique patients seen (growth proxy)
f06_patient_growth.interp: The 5,000 appointments involve 4,443 distinct patients (22.2% of the register); 510 patients visited more than once. About 370 new patients appear per month with no visible acceleration, which is what an unrelated random draw from the register would produce. Registration dates are not recorded, so first-appointment month is only a proxy for patient growth.

f07_diagnoses.title: Diagnosis frequency (60,000 diagnoses)
f07_diagnoses.interp: Five diagnoses share the caseload almost equally — Gastritis leads with 20.3% and Upper Respiratory Infection trails with 19.6%. Severity is split roughly in thirds (severe 33.3%), and the severity mix is the same for every disease (χ² p = 0.187). A one-third severe rate is far higher than in usual primary-care case-mix; management should confirm how severity is coded.

f08_labs_rx.title: Laboratory test volume
f08_labs_rx.interp: Lab volume is evenly spread over four tests (CBC, Glucose, Malaria, Urinalysis; 24%–25% each) and 50% of results are abnormal (range 50–51% by test). Prescribing follows diagnosis exactly — 100% of prescriptions match the standard drug for the diagnosis (Metformin for diabetes, Amlodipine for hypertension, Omeprazole for gastritis, Amoxicillin for URI, Artemether-Lumefantrine for malaria) — so Amlodipine leads only because it follows the diagnosis mix. Laboratory ordering, by contrast, is unrelated to diagnosis (χ² p = 0.366): malaria patients are not more likely to receive a malaria test, which management should review as a possible test-ordering or data-capture gap.

f09_admissions_referrals.title: Monthly admission and referral rate
f09_admissions_referrals.interp: 11.7% of appointments end in admission (586 of 5,000) with a mean stay of 5.5 days; stay lengths 1–10 days are equally likely (χ² p = 0.159). Monthly admission rates bounce between 8.2% and 14.7% with no trend (Spearman ρ = 0.31, p = 0.319). Referrals touch 8.3% of appointments; destinations range 201–258 referrals per facility and are statistically even (χ² p = 0.299), so no facility acts as a referral hub.

f10_staff_workload.title: Appointments per doctor (350 doctors)
f10_staff_workload.interp: Doctors handle 14.3 appointments each on average (range 5–28); the variance-to-mean ratio is 0.95, i.e. almost exactly what random assignment (Poisson ≈ 1.0) would produce, so there is no systematic overload of particular doctors. Appointments per nurse range 6.2–7.9 across facilities (every facility has 35–35 nurses).

f11_facility_utilisation.title: Facility utilisation: appointments by facility
f11_facility_utilisation.interp: Facility volumes run from 217 (HF019) to 278 (HF013) appointments — a 28% gap — which are not significantly different from equal shares (χ² p = 0.052; borderline). Staffing is nearly identical everywhere (61–64 staff per facility), so the load per staff member differs only through patient volume: 220 to 290 staff per 1,000 patients seen, and staff numbers do not track patient volume (Spearman ρ = -0.10, p = 0.689).

f12_capacity.title: Bed occupancy – lower-bound estimate
f12_capacity.interp: All 2,000 beds (100 per facility, 5 per room) carry the status 'Available', so occupancy cannot be read directly. Using admission length-of-stay, recorded admissions fill only about 3.8% of annual bed-days at system level — far below any realistic figure, which suggests the Admissions extract is a sample. Equipment is one generic line per department (20 per department type), so equipment shortages cannot be measured. The department-by-month heatmap shows no obvious seasonal surge in any department type.

f13_revenue_trend.title: Monthly revenue (Revenue_Summary)
f13_revenue_trend.interp: Revenue totals 1.13 bn RWF for 2026 (mean 94 M/month) but is volatile — coefficient of variation 27%, from 67 M in December to 146 M in September. Revenue per appointment swings between 13k and 32k RWF, and monthly revenue is only weakly related to monthly appointments (r = 0.28, p = 0.370), so revenue is driven by billing size at least as much as by visit counts.

f14_billing_claims_payments.title: Billing amount distribution (60,000 bills)
f14_billing_claims_payments.interp: Bills are uniformly spread between 10k and 300k RWF (mean 155k). Of 9.31 bn billed, 8.39 bn has been paid, leaving 0.92 bn (9.9%) outstanding. The recorded Status field is not a reliable guide: bills marked 'Paid', 'Partially Paid' and 'Pending' have the same average payment ratio (≈90% in each group). Radiant generates the highest claim value (1.24 bn). Only 50% of claims are approved, and approval does not differ significantly across providers (χ² p = 0.077).

f15_revenue_by_unit.title: Billed revenue by department type (5,000-appointment cohort)
f15_revenue_by_unit.interp: Within the 5,000-appointment cohort (771 M RWF billed), Cardiology bills the most (86 M) and HF011 is the top facility (44 M). Differences are driven by appointment counts, not price: average bill per appointment does not differ significantly across departments (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.471), facilities (p = 0.303) or diagnoses (p = 0.555). Services are not linked to appointments in the data, so diagnosis is used as the service-line proxy; true 'revenue by service' needs a ServiceID on the bill.

f16_satisfaction.title: Satisfaction rating distribution (21,064)
f16_satisfaction.interp: The average rating is 2.99 out of 5 and all five ratings are about equally common (≈20% each); 35% of encounters have feedback. The written comment tells us nothing about the score — a rating of 1 is as likely to carry 'Excellent' as 'Poor' (χ² p = 0.904) — so feedback capture should be reviewed. Monthly shares of poor and excellent ratings fluctuate without trend (Spearman p = 0.83 and 0.83).

f17_satisfaction_comparison.title: Mean satisfaction by facility (95% CI)
f17_satisfaction_comparison.interp: Facility means run from 2.76 (HF020) to 3.19 (HF011) and department-type means from 2.76 to 3.02, but with only ~89 rated visits per facility every confidence interval includes the overall mean (2.93). Kruskal-Wallis finds no significant difference across facilities (p = 0.795) or departments (p = 0.878). Rankings of 'best' and 'worst' sites are therefore not statistically defensible with the current data.

f18_distributions.title: Distributions of key numeric variables (dashed = median, dotted = quartiles)
f18_distributions.interp: None of the key variables is bell-shaped: patient age, length of stay and staff experience are flat across their range, and bill amount is statistically indistinguishable from a uniform distribution (KS p = 0.92), while BMI is right-skewed (skew 0.46; median 29.2, mean 30.0) with 0.2% of patients above the upper box-plot fence. Because the data are not normal, rank-based tests (Mann-Whitney, Kruskal-Wallis, Spearman) are used alongside parametric ones in the sections that follow. The median bill is 155k RWF.

f19_violins.title: Bill amount by disease severity
f19_violins.interp: Violin shapes are essentially identical across groups: bills do not differ by severity (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.639) — severe cases are not billed more than mild ones, which is clinically unexpected; BMI does not differ by chronic condition (p = 0.904); and satisfaction does not differ by visit type (p = 0.680). Where real-world relationships should exist (severity→cost, obesity→diabetes/hypertension) none is present.

f20_correlation_heatmap.title: Spearman correlation heatmap — encounter master (pairwise complete observations)
f20_correlation_heatmap.interp: Of 120 variable pairs only 9 reach p < 0.05 unadjusted (about 6 are expected by pure chance), and 2 survive Holm correction. The pairs that survive Holm correction are arithmetic ones (Bill amount ↔ Amount paid (ρ = 0.91); Amount paid ↔ Paid ÷ billed (ρ = 0.38)). Every clinically meaningful pair — age, BMI, chronic disease, severity, admission, bill, rating — is |ρ| < 0.13. Key drivers that would normally separate patient groups are absent, which limits what any predictive model can achieve.

f21_pairplot.title: Pair plot — age, BMI, bill amount, doctor experience by severity
f21_pairplot.interp: The scatter panels form rectangular clouds with no slope, the density curves on the diagonal overlap for all three severity levels, and no cluster of points separates Severe from Mild cases. Age, BMI, bill size and the treating doctor's experience are statistically independent of each other and of severity in this data.

f22_age_admission_bill_los.title: Admission rate by age group (95% CI)
f22_age_admission_bill_los.interp: Admission rates by age group stay within noise of the 11.7% average (highest 13.9% in 50–64); the age–admission correlation is 0.021 (p = 0.129) and the age–bill correlation -0.003 (p = 0.859). Mean length of stay is 5.3–5.9 days across diagnoses with overlapping intervals (Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.538). Older patients are not admitted more often, billed more, or kept longer.

f23_admission_drivers.title: Association of each factor with admission
f23_admission_drivers.interp: Of 26 candidate factors, 2 reach p < 0.05 before correction (about 1 expected by chance) and 0 after Holm correction. The strongest signal is 'High-risk patient flag' (raw p = 0.022, effect size 0.032), which is negligible in size. No demographic, clinical or operational factor can be confirmed as a driver of admission, so admission in this data is best described as unexplained by recorded variables.

f24_chronic_risk_groups.title: Chronic-disease prevalence by patient group with 95% Wilson CI (red = interval excludes overall 74.6%)
f24_chronic_risk_groups.interp: Among 41 patient groups, 3 have a prevalence interval that excludes the overall 74.6% (about 2 would be expected by chance). The highest-prevalence group is Blood group = A+ (77.4%, n = 2,889), only 2.8 points above average. Only Blood group survives Holm correction (Cramér's V = 0.033, a negligible effect), so no group can be called materially more at risk.

f25_chronic_odds_ratios.title: Logistic regression: odds ratios for any chronic disease (95% bootstrap CI)
f25_chronic_odds_ratios.interp: Cross-validated AUC for predicting chronic disease from age, BMI, gender, marital status, education, occupation, province and blood group is 0.512 ± 0.007 (0.5 = coin-flip). Only 6 of 26 odds ratios have an interval that excludes 1 (about 1 expected by chance). With an AUC this close to 0.5, the recorded demographics cannot meaningfully identify who is at risk of chronic disease.

f26_hypothesis_summary.title: Hypothesis tests at a glance (red = significant at α = 0.05)
f26_hypothesis_summary.interp: 0 of 15 tests reject the null hypothesis at α = 0.05; after Holm correction 0 remain. None of the outcome-related comparisons — admission, satisfaction, length of stay, billing — shows a significant difference, so the data give no evidence that these outcomes vary by the factors tested. The nearest to significance are H3 (admission by age group, p = 0.065) and H12 (claim approval by provider, p = 0.077); neither reaches α = 0.05.

f27_forecast_visits.title: Monthly patient visits — 12-month forecast (Simple exp. smoothing)
f27_forecast_visits.interp: Monthly visits fluctuate around 5,067 with no trend (Spearman ρ = -0.14, p = 0.665) and no significant month-to-month autocorrelation (lag-1 = -0.41, inside the ±0.57 noise band). The best back-tested model is 'Simple exp. smoothing' — only marginally better than the plain average (MAPE 14.0% vs 15.3%) — and forecasts ≈4,975 visits a month for 2027 (59,701 for the year, -1.8% versus 2026). Honest answer to 'can demand be forecast accurately?': only at the level of a stable average — typical monthly error is ±14% and the 95% band is ±1,918 visits (39%). A real seasonal model needs at least 24 months of history.

f28_forecast_revenue.title: Monthly revenue — 12-month forecast (Simple exp. smoothing)
f28_forecast_revenue.interp: Revenue shows no detectable trend (Spearman ρ = -0.17, p = 0.587; lag-1 autocorrelation -0.42). The best back-tested model is 'Simple exp. smoothing' (MAPE 26%), giving ≈92 M RWF per month and 1.10 bn RWF for 2027 (-2.6% vs 2026's 1.13 bn). Uncertainty is large — the 95% band is ±62 M per month (±68%) — because single months such as Sep-2026 (146 M) and Dec-2026 (67 M) are far from the average. Use the 2027 figure as a budget baseline, not a monthly target.

f29_department_workload_forecast.title: Forecast 2027 visits per month by department type
f29_department_workload_forecast.interp: Demand is spread almost evenly over the ten department types (9.3%–10.9% of visits; χ² for equal shares p = 0.490) and shows no month-of-year pattern by department (χ² p = 0.502). With clinician numbers also equal, forecast workload indices lie between 93 and 109; the highest is Cardiology (index 109, simulated probability of exceeding the 115 line 38%). Differences between types are not statistically significant, so no department type is clearly headed for overload; the risk is spread thinly and is dominated by random variation in monthly demand, so staffing decisions should rely on monitoring (rolling 3-month load) rather than a fixed forecast.

f30_admission_model.title: Cross-validated AUC by model and feature set
f30_admission_model.interp: Best cross-validated AUC is 0.514 (Logistic regression, feature set A) — at or barely above chance (0.5); the label-shuffling test gives p = 0.317, so it is indistinguishable from chance. Hold-out AUC 0.529 (95% CI 0.47–0.59). Adding diagnosis, severity, labs, medication and referral does not improve on booking-time information. Calibration: predicted risks cluster near the 11.7% base rate; observed admission is 16.0% in the top-risk quintile and 12.0% in the lowest, a gap that is within sampling noise for only 200 patients per quintile — no usable risk stratification. Admissions in this data cannot be predicted from the recorded variables.

f31_admission_importance.title: Permutation importance — admission model (drop in hold-out AUC when feature is shuffled)
f31_admission_importance.interp: Even the most 'important' feature (DepartmentName) changes hold-out AUC by only 0.011, and most bars straddle zero (error bars = SD over 15 shuffles). Importance values this small indicate noise-fitting rather than genuine drivers, matching the factor screen in section 4.3.

f32_satisfaction_model.title: Cross-validated R² for predicting rating
f32_satisfaction_model.interp: No model predicts satisfaction: the best cross-validated R² of any real model is -0.001 (Gradient boosting, Scope 1 – all feedback) — zero or negative means no better than always guessing the average rating (≈2.93). Classifying 'satisfied' (rating ≥ 4) gives AUC 0.50–0.51. The label-shuffle test for the cohort model is p = 0.436. Clinical, billing, operational and demographic variables carry no information about the rating, so improving satisfaction needs new data — waiting time, staff attitude, cleanliness, drug availability — not a better model.

f33_patient_clusters.title: Patients: silhouette vs null, by number of clusters
f33_patient_clusters.interp: The only structure K-Means finds is the set of mutually exclusive chronic-condition indicators: silhouette peaks at 0.28 (k = 8) versus 0.21 for shuffled data, and the gap comes from those binary variables, not from age, BMI, gender or visit behaviour, which show no grouping. The four-segment solution is therefore the three chronic-condition groups (asthma, hypertension, diabetes; each ≈4,992 patients and 38–39% meeting the high-risk rule) and the no-chronic-disease group (18% high-risk). Segments do not differ in admission rate (χ² p = 0.720), so they help target outreach but add no outcome information beyond the chronic-condition label.

f34_facility_clusters.title: Ward hierarchical clustering of facilities
f34_facility_clusters.interp: Facilities split into 2 groups (silhouette 0.19; shuffled-data chance of doing this well p = 0.005), but the grouping is consistent across methods (ARI 0.80). Cluster 1 = high volume, high load per clinician, low staff ratio; cluster 2 = low volume, low load per clinician, high staff ratio — i.e. the split rests on three mechanically linked volume measures (appointments, load per clinician, staff per 1,000 patients), not on quality or outcomes. The Performance Score (scaled 0–100 by construction; HF001 highest, HF007 lowest) is built from components that rest on only ~89 ratings and ~247 appointments per site, so rank differences are not statistically reliable — use clusters to pick peer groups for comparison, not to rank.

f35_department_clusters.title: Departments: silhouette vs null
f35_department_clusters.interp: Department profiles form a largely continuous cloud rather than separate groups (best silhouette 0.14, only slightly above 0.10 for shuffled data), and segments are unrelated to department type (χ² p = 0.604). The four-segment split still gives management a practical triage list: segments with high volume and high load per clinician (see heat-map rows with positive 'Volume' and 'Load/clin.') are the first candidates for staffing review, but these profiles rest on ~25 appointments per department and should be re-estimated as more data accrue.

f36_pca.title: Patients: scree plot and cumulative variance
f36_pca.interp: Patient data need 6 of 10 components to retain 80% of variance (7 for 90%); the first component explains 21% versus 10% for shuffled data — the excess comes from variables that are built from each other — so beyond those built-in links the variables are independent and cannot be compressed much. PC1 is dominated by BMI, WeightKg, RiskScore (loadings +0.63, +0.54, +0.39), reflecting arithmetic links between variables (BMI is computed from height and weight; the risk score from age, BMI and chronic disease). Facility measures need 5 of 12 components for 80% (7 for 90%) because 20 sites × 12 noisy measures leave little shared structure. PCA therefore offers little dimensionality reduction here; it is retained as a diagnostic that confirms the absence of hidden low-dimensional drivers.
